News.title: Labour’s defence investment fund will be £14BILLION short of what’s needed ‘to keep nation safe’
News.content:
LABOUR’S UK defence ­investment fund is around £14billion short of what Forces chiefs insist they need to keep the nation safe.

New Defence Secretary Dan Jarvis lost the battle with Chancellor Rachel Reeves over the long-awaited Defence Investment Plan (DIP), which was hoped to plug a £28billion black hole in the Ministry of Defence’s accounts.





Yesterday Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer announced ­£5billion for drones over four years as part of the expected £14.5billion settlement.

But most of that money was announced last year, with defence insiders admitting: “Only £1billion is new money.”

And a defence source slammed Mr Starmer’s announcement, saying that the £5billion injection was less than two per cent of the MoD’s budget over the next four years.

They said: “This is hardly a revolution. It is utter f*****g waffle. We are still not learning the lessons from Ukraine.”



It is understood Mr ­Jarvis, who was a major in the Parachute Regiment, managed to secure an extra £1billion for the MoD but Ms Reeves refused to make major cuts elsewhere to properly fund defence.

It comes amid warnings that ­Britain has become a laughing stock among Nato allies over its failure to meet defence promises.

The Chief of the Defence Staff Sir Richard Knighton warned this month that training and missions will have to be cut.

And Defence Secretary John Healey and Armed Forces Minister Al Carns both quit this month in protest at constraints in the investment fund.



Sir Keir had originally offered the MoD an extra £13.5billion over the next four years.

But MoD insiders said the figure was only £10billion of new money once “Treasury trickery” had been taken into account.

Yesterday the PM insisted the £5billion for drones was a “game-changing investment”.

He said: “It will strengthen our Armed Forces on land, at sea and in the air, ensuring our servicemen and women have the cutting-edge capabilities they need to deter evolving threats and keep British people safe.”

The MoD said drones would range from “highly complex autonomous mine-hunting drones to small quadcopter tactical drones, and low-cost kamikaze one-way attack drones”.

News.title: Asylum seekers will be forced to PAY BACK cost of their accommodation under new student loan-style scheme
News.content:
MIGRANTS will be forced to pay back the cost of their accommodation in a student loan-style scheme — and will be stopped from getting settled status until they do.

Those who have been put up at taxpayers’ expense will be made to pay off part of their board and lodgings once they start earning above a certain threshold, the Government will announce today.





The full amount, expected to be about £10,000, must be paid off before anyone can apply for settled status under the Home Office plans.

It is part of the Immigration and Asylum Bill to be introduced to Parliament today.

Dr Madeleine Sumption, director of the Migration Observatory at the University of Oxford, said it was likely that only a relatively small share of people granted asylum would earn enough to pay towards the scheme.

It might also discourage asylum seekers from working once they got refugee status to avoid the cost, she said.



Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood said: “The cost of asylum accommodation on the British taxpayer is too high. We have already reduced asylum costs by £1billion, but it is also right that we ask those who can contribute to do so.

“Receiving asylum support is a right, but it is also a responsibility. Once people can contribute and repay the generosity of the British people, we expect them to do so.”

The Government said it spent £4billion on accommodation and support for asylum seekers last year.

The Home Office estimates the average cost per person per night of accommodating asylum seekers is £23.25 in dispersal accommodation and £144 in hotels.



Meanwhile, subsistence payments range from £9.95 to £49.18 a person a week.

News.title: Andy Burnham is a pedlar of illusions who wants to turn the clock back to the dark days of the 1970s
News.content:
THE King of the North has spoken. Manchester’s Municipal Messiah has handed down his sacred text, prompting another wave of gushing praise from the Labour faithful.

In his first major speech since he announced his bid for the party leadership and effectively forced Sir Keir Starmer to quit as Prime Minister, Andy Burnham presented himself as the heroic architect of a prosperous, dynamic new Britain.





A country where every high street will flourish and “every postcode” will have good growth.

This remarkable transformation, he explained, will be achieved by the “biggest rebalancing of power our country has ever seen”, where control of key services such as skills education, house building, regeneration and welfare are to be transferred to local bodies and mayors.

In his speech, Burnham was long on uplifting rhetoric but short on gritty detail.

He is asking us to put our faith in him on the basis of wishful thinking rather than hard evidence.

For a politician who aspires to the premiership, his record is distinctly thin.

If, as now seems almost certain, he succeeds Sir Keir in just three weeks’ time, he will be the first Prime Minister in the history of British democracy not to have been the official Leader of the Opposition or to have held one of the three great offices of state as either Home Secretary or Chancellor or Foreign Secretary.

His supporters counter that he has been a successful Mayor of Greater Manchester since 2017.

In this role, he has presided over a local economic growth rate of 3.1 per cent, twice the national average, while he also brought the privatised local transport network in Greater Manchester under municipal control, a move that did wonders for his popularity but not for the transport authority’s balance sheet.



The subsidy for the local bus system amounts to £220million this year.

Indeed, there are many critics who think that Burnham is no more than a pedlar of illusions, whose claims to have worked a miracle in Manchester are built on implausible data and feelgood propaganda.

But it is also fair to ask how relevant Burnham’s experience as mayor is to the premiership.

Running a city, after all, is very different to running a country.

A mayor is in the advantageous position of being able to take credit for the policy successes but can blame the Government for the failures.

As Ben Houchen, Tory Mayor of Teesside, puts it, Burnham “is engaged in the politics of the perpetual announcement: New funds, new projects, new ambitions, all received with something approaching reverence in Greater Manchester”.



But ruling a country is much harder.

The head of the government can’t hide behind gimmickry or pass the blame to others. In the words of the famous notice President Harry Truman put on his desk in the White House, “the buck stops here”.

It is not clear that Burnham has either the stomach for tough decisions, or the right policy agenda for Britain’s needs.



At the heart of yesterday’s speech, Burnham displayed his naive belief in two political theories, both of them related to his experience as Greater Manchester’s mayor.

The first is his attachment to decentralisation.

In Burnham’s world, the local town hall is better at taking decisions than remote Whitehall.

But there is no real proof of this.

Local councils are notorious for their waste, inefficiency, mismanagement and top-heavy staffing structures.



In 2024, for instance, Transport for London had, incredibly, 2,217 staff on more than £100,000 a year, an increase of 68 per cent on the previous year.

Local authorities were at the forefront of the cover-up over grooming gangs, just as several town halls have been dragged to the brink of bankruptcy by foolish speculative investments.

The second strand of Burnham’s credulous thinking is his blind worship of the public sector, despite its dismal record on the delivery of services.

So many big capital projects, such as the HS2 rail link, have been grossly over budget, while far too much NHS funding disappears down a black hole.

Productivity and innovation are far too low in this sector, sick leave and union power too high.



Yet Burnham wants to turn the clock to the dark days of the 1970s, when large sections of the economy were nationalised and the unions were invited into No10 for beer and sandwiches.

Tellingly, he has already accepted £20,000 from three trade unions for his leadership campaign.

But neither decentralisation nor nationalisation will come cheap.



Burnham’s grand vision of new efficiencies generated by public and local control is just the stuff of fantasies.

There will be huge extra costs from the creation of new regional assemblies, new mayoralties and new tiers of bureaucrats.

Burnham also set out his plan yesterday for yet another extension of officialdom, when he proposed a new “No10 of the North” to act as the “nerve centre” for his constitutional experiment.

To pay for this, taxes will have to go up, even though the overall burden is at its highest level since the 1940s.

And more cash will to be found for some of his other proposals, like a major overhaul of business rates.



It is inevitable that the south-east of England will have to fork out more, particularly if the new Prime Minister carries through his threat to add extra council tax bands to reflect the higher property values in the capital and the wider region.

In the longer term, Burnham is looking at two other changes which will punish people in this region even more: The replacement of the council tax and stamp duty with an annual tax on land values, plus the devolution of some income tax-raising powers to regional bodies.

But socialists like Burnham should recognise that the streets of London are not paved with gold.

There are worryingly high levels of poverty and unemployment in the capital, just as Britain’s most deprived constituency, Clacton, is in the South East.

Burnham likes to talk about rebalancing, but he might make a start by ending the institutional habit of treating the South East as a milch cow.



Devolution can be a nightmare in another way.

Extra cash and powers allow mavericks to indulge ideological extremism, as we see with a phalanx of disastrous mayors in the US, such as the socialist Zohran Mamdani in New York and Katie Wilson in Seattle.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

We had the same here in the 1980s with Red Ken Livingstone in London.

Get ready for the King of the North to unleash a new round of municipal mayhem.

News.title: Fury as ‘unpatriotic’ Starmer yet to fly England flag outside No10 during World Cup
News.content:
SIR Keir Starmer has faced furious backlash after failing to fly the St George’s Cross outside No 10.

The outgoing Labour Prime Minister was branded as unpatriotic for snubbing the England squad as they kicked off their World Cup campaign in the group stages.





Tory party chairman Kevin Hollinrake accused the PM of being “just another Labour Party plastic patriot” calling for him to “show some backbone”.

The North Yorkshire MP said: “Keir Starmer claims to love his country but won’t fly the England flag for the World Cup.

“He should show some backbone and pride in our flag and our history. These are the things that bring us together.

“Regardless of what Starmer and his colleagues think, millions of us will be cheering the England team on to the final whistle in all of their games.”



Flying the St George’s Cross at Downing Street became a tradition under David Cameron who raised the flag for the entirety of the Three Lions’ 2010 World Cup campaign in South Africa.

The same year, then local government minister Grant Shapps called for councils across England to show their support “to avoid accusations of being overzealous or spoilsports”.

Sir Keir previously referred to the England flag as “an expression of our values and our patriotism”.

During St George’s Day celebrations last year he said: “We should be proud of that flag, we must never concede it”.



A spokesperson for No 10 confirmed that they intended to fly the England flag if the team progressed to the knockout stages.

After finishing top of their group, Thomas Tuchel’s men now face the Democratic Republic of Congo on Wednesday in the first knockout game of the tournament.

News.title: Fury as 83 asylum seekers being moved into £250k newbuild homes on village estate ‘meant for social housing’
News.content:
A TOTAL of 83 asylum seekers are to be moved in to £250,000 homes on an estate dubbed “Migrant Street”.

Twenty-one smart newbuild houses have been earmarked for the families.





But one local in Stoke Heath, Shropshire, said: “It’s bang out of order.

“It doesn’t feel fair that these people will be living in shiny new homes free of charge, which hard-working local folk could never afford.”

Outraged villagers claim they have been lied to over plans to move the asylum seekers into the newbuild homes — and have vowed to fight the scheme.

They say they were told the new development would be affordable housing. But they have since learned that 21 homes in the Shropshire village of Stoke Heath have been earmarked for asylum seekers.



One migrant family is understood to have already moved into one of the properties, with more expected to arrive in the coming weeks.

Emma O’Sullivan, 30, said: “We were told that the new development would be social houses, which was fine, but no one moved in for a year.



“Now we’re told they will be used for asylum seekers and they’re not part of the social housing at all. We feel like we’ve been lied to.

“I’ve got three teenage girls and we’re really worried. It’s not who they are, it’s how many there are. It’ll overload the infrastructure. There are only two primary schools in the area so if they’re all families that’s going to flood the ­primary schools. It’s just, ‘They’re here, put up with them’.”

Melanie Almond said: “It was like a bomb’s gone off and you’ve got ten minutes to get out. It was a complete shock. I found out on the internet. We couldn’t believe it.”

Another local said: “It’s bang out of order and people now call it ‘Migrant Street’, which will be pretty accurate. It doesn’t feel fair that these people will be living in shiny new homes free of charge, which hard-working local folk could never afford.”

Army veteran John “Basil” Brockhurst was angry the new housing was not being used for people struggling on the poverty line. He said: “To me there’s a lot more people that need brand new housing rather than people who make out they come from far away countries.”



The area’s Tory MP Mark Pritchard has called the village a “completely inappropriate location” for the plans. He said: “Stoke Heath is an isolated rural location with very few public services.

“This is the wrong location and at the wrong scale. I will fight these ill-conceived plans all the way.”

Shropshire Council has written to Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood to “raise our strong concerns about this location and are awaiting a response before considering any further action”.



Police and Crime Commissioner of West Mercia John-Paul Campion called the plan “wholly inappropriate”.

The Government insists the move is part of a wider strategy to cut costs and reduce hotel use by 2029, instead relocating people into “properties and ex-military sites”.

As of March, 20,885 asylum seekers were in hotel rooms and 72,768 were in other accommodation such as houses in multiple occupation and camps as they waited for their claims to be processed.

Serco, the outsourcing company responsible for housing asylum seekers and migrants in the West Midlands, said: “We work under the direction of the Home Office, who decide where ­people are placed, based on overall national demand.

“The Home Office determines how many people are to be accommodated in each local authority area and instruct us accordingly.”



The Home Office said: “This Government is restoring order to the system by making record levels of asylum decisions, cutting claims by 12 per cent and increasing removals of illegal migrants by 41 per cent.

“We are working closely with local authorities to ramp up the closure of asylum hotels across the UK.

Hotel numbers have more than halved since their peak and instead we are scaling up the use of large, basic accommodation for illegal migrants to reduce community impact.”

News.title: Andy Burnham’s speech proves he’s ready to seize power without a proper plan for Government
News.content:
False prophet

THE Sun has repeatedly warned that presumptive Prime Minister Andy Burnham was getting ready to seize power without a proper plan for Government.

His much-hyped speech proved he still hasn’t got one. Instead he served up the usual guff about “hope” and made wild promises which would take decades to deliver — if ever.





Burnham said he wanted to implement the biggest devolution of power from Downing Street to the cities and regions, including a gimmick to create a No10 North in Manchester. But if devolution was the answer, why is Scotland drowning in debt and Wales so poor?

There was also a pledge for a massive building programme of council houses — but no explanation of how he’ll pay for it. Vague words about taking water and energy “into public control” were similarly lacking in detail.

Crucially, Burnham made NO mention of reforming welfare, getting kids into work, cutting national debt or boosting defence. What help is he going to give hard-working, over-taxed families?

The public remains in the dark about how he will fix their priorities.



Burnham’s promises will, however, delight the left-dominated public sector by leading to MORE Government.

Labour MPs — increasingly acting like crazed cult members — will follow a man who ousted an elected PM and now refuses a General Election while lecturing us about “broken politics”.

Burnham repeatedly asked us to “imagine” a new Britain, delivering “good growth in every postcode”.

But voters weary of political over-promising will be wary of what could be yet another false prophet.



Tax breaks

ANDY Burnham said working families deserved to be able to afford a hard-earned holiday.

Yet the current Labour Government is determined to make it more expensive for them by slapping a tax on a British break. Kemi Badenoch is right to ban Tory mayors from imposing it.

When will Burnham recognise the unfairness of raiding working family budgets to pay for welfare?

Flagging PM

KEIR Starmer once said the following about the Cross of St George.

“We should be proud of that flag, we must never concede it, because it is an expression of our values and patriotism.”



Quite right. So why fail to fly the England flag over Downing Street during England’s World Cup matches?

Bafflingly, Number Ten insists it will only be raised for knockout games, starting with DR Congo tomorrow.

Could it be that the PM and his team simply forgot?

News.title: Huge blast rocks Monaco after booby-trapped backpack explodes leaving ‘Ukrainian oligarch’ fighting for life
News.content:
A SUSPECT is on the run after a huge explosion injured three Ukrainians in Monaco, leaving two of them fighting for their lives in critical condition.

Ukrainian oligarch Vadim Ermolaev has been left fighting for his life in critical condition after the explosion, sources told French media.





Vadim is the 23rd richest man in Ukraine, according to Forbes.

Police said a suspect was caught on CCTV cameras putting a backpack down before fleeing the scene on foot towards the French border.

The victims were said to be three Ukrainians of the same family, with two fighting for their lives after the explosion.

A 13-year-old boy is in stable condition, but his two parents in their 50s and 60s were left in critical condition after the “attack”.

The blast rocked a residential building on a street bordering France around 9pm.

The suspect was spotted fleeing towards the border with the nearby French town of Beausoleil.

One Monaco resident who heard the explosion told The Sun it sounded “like if thunder was coming from behind the mountains”.

A suspect was spotted placing a bag down then leaving, perhaps disappearing into France.



Blood was pictured on the steps of the building, which The Sun has decided to pixelate for the privacy of any victims.



Casualties from the explosion are likely, officials said.

It was described as an “attack” by Mayor of Nice Eric Ciotti.

He wrote on X: “The attack carried out this evening is a tragedy that has hit Monaco.

“Thoughts for the victims, their families, and the people of Monaco.

“Total support for the security forces and emergency services mobilised.”



There has been no official confirmation if this was a terror attack.

Monaco’s Minister of State Christophe Mirmand told AFP: “This is likely an attack.”

He added that the bags planted at the scene contained bolts.

Police said Monaco’s red plan had been activated, with officers conducting checks at the border with France as the suspected attacker remained at large.

One local reported hearing the explosion, writing on social media: “At first, I thought it was the start of a storm, but the noise was incredibly loud.”



President of the neighbouring French region’s council Charles Ange Ginésy, wrote on X: “In the face of the attack that occurred in Monaco this evening, I express my deep solidarity with the victims, their families, and the people of Monaco.
